FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Assess the preoperative management of anemia.
Review intraoperative techniques to reduce blood loss.
Evaluate postoperative protocols to manage/reduce blood loss.
Determine methods that minimize blood loss and unnecessary blood transfusions while
ensuring safe and effective patient care.
Overview
Total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) are among the most commonly
performed procedures in orthopaedic surgery. Historically, THA and TKA have been associated
with substantial blood loss and increased blood transfusion requirements. In the past,

perioperative blood loss has been reported to be between 300 mL and 1 L, with blood
transfusion rates as high as 30% and 25% during THA and TKA, respectively.1,2
Blood transfusions have been associated with several postoperative complications, including
periprosthetic joint infection, increased hospital length of stay, and an increase in overall
episode-of-care costs.3
Multiple strategies have been developed to reduce intraoperative blood loss and the need for
blood transfusion.4,5 With the implementation of tranexamic acid (TXA), the rate of blood
transfusion after TKA currently is approximately 1%.6
Reducing the risk of postoperative hematoma also is important to decrease intravascular
blood volume loss because this negatively affects joint mobility.7
The guidelines of the American Association of Blood Banks suggest adherence to a strict
transfusion trigger for stable, hospitalized patients of less than or equal to 7 g/dL for low-risk
patients and less than or equal to 8 g/dL for patients with known cardiovascular disease.8
Preoperative Management
Preoperative Evaluation
Preoperative strategies for a patient undergoing THA or TKA include optimization of
hemoglobin levels to enable patients to better tolerate the physiologic stress associated with
acute blood loss anemia from surgery3 (Resource 1). 
A preoperative evaluation of the patient should take place 3 weeks preoperative to allow
enough time for appropriate intervention if necessary. The ideal preoperative process is to
develop a patient-specific preoperative blood management plan based on preoperative
hemoglobin status, underlying etiology for anemia, and associated comorbidities that may
influence perioperative surgical risk.9
For patients with chronic anemia, consultation with a medical physician and a hematologist is
recommended for a comprehensive evaluation.
Causes of Chronic Anemia
Iron deficiency anemia
Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency
Chronic disease/inflammation
Hemolytic anemia

Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

Causes of Chronic Anemia
World Health Organization criteria for anemia in men and women are hemoglobin levels
less than 13 and less than 12 g/dL, respectively.
Erythropoiesis in adults takes place in the bone marrow under the influence of
erythroid-specific growth factor (erythropoietin [EPO]). EPO is a true endocrine hormone
produced in the kidney by cells that sense adequacy of tissue oxygenation relative to
metabolic activity.
The reticulocyte still has a ribosomal network and can be stained. Reticulocyte retains its
ribosomal network for 4 days (3 days in bone marrow and 1 day in peripheral blood). The
resulting mature red blood cell (RBC) circulates for 110 to 120 days, after which time it is
removed from the circulation by macrophages. Under steady-state conditions, the rate
of RBC production equals the rate of RBC loss. Reticulocytes normally survive in the
circulation for 1 day. Under steady-state conditions reticulocytes represent 1% of total
circulating RBCs.
Normal bone marrow replete with iron, folate, and cobalamin can increase
erythropoiesis in response to EPO by approximately fivefold in adults.
A 79-kg adult with acute bleeding of 750 mL may have normal hemoglobin and
hematocrit levels because of volume depletion. During the ensuing 48 hours, most of the
total blood volume deficit will be replaced with fluids; only at these later times will the
hemoglobin and hematocrit levels reflect blood loss.
Clinical Consequences
Signs and symptoms of anemia depend on the degree of anemia and the rate at which it has
evolved.

Lethargy, confusion, fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, dizziness

Clinical Consequences
If bone marrow is otherwise healthy, it will respond to anemia by increasing the number
of RBC precursors and hastening progression to reticulocytes. After an acute drop in
hemoglobin level, reticulocytes generally appear in the peripheral blood within a few
days to 2 weeks. Therefore, an increased reticulocyte count indicates that the bone
marrow can produce RBCs. The more common causes for a decrease in effective RBC
production include the following:
Lack of nutrients, such as vitamin B12 and iron. Iron deficiency is commonly the result
of blood loss.
Low levels of trophic hormones that stimulate RBC production, such as EPO (eg,
chronic renal failure), thyroid hormones (eg, hypothyroidism), and androgens
(hypogonadism)
Anemia of chronic disease, also known as anemia of inflammation, is associated with
infectious, inflammatory, or malignant disorders and is characterized by reduced
availability of iron because of decreased absorption of iron from the gastrointestinal
tract and decreased release of iron from macrophages, a relative reduction in EPO
levels, and a mild reduction in RBC life span.
Blood loss is the most common cause of anemia; however, it often is difficult to
quantify.
Iron and Vitamin Supplementation
Whether vitamin supplementation and the administration of iron preoperatively can minimize
the likelihood of transfusion after major surgery remains unclear.10,11
Adverse effects of these supplements include constipation, heartburn, and abdominal pain.
Routine administration of iron is not supported unless anemia is attributed to low iron levels.3
In patients with iron deficiency anemia, serum iron and ferritin concentrations are decreased.
This is contrary to anemia in patients with chronic disease, in which ferritin concentration is

increased. In addition, in anemia in patients with chronic disease, serum folic acid and vitamin
B12 concentrations are decreased, dissimilar from patients with iron deficiency anemia, in
whom these levels remain normal.
The maximum rate of absorption of 100 mg of oral iron is 20% to 25% and is reached only in
the late stage of iron deficiency.12
If faster repletion is desired in patients with iron deficiency anemia, intravenous
administration is the preferred route. Regardless, oral iron is readily available, inexpensive,
and convenient, making it a viable treatment option.12
Focus on causal management is the primary treatment option for anemia in patients with
chronic disease.13
Regardless, extensive iron (oral or intravenous), vitamin C, folic acid, and vitamin B12
supplementation should be considered.13
Erythropoietin
EPO is a hypoxia-induced cytokine that stimulates erythropoiesis via the promotion of
erythroid precursor cell proliferation and differentiation. Its primary role involves prevention
of programmed cell death (apoptosis of erythrocyte precursors).14,15
The administration of EPO requires advance notice to coordinate the timing of injection.
The most common administration protocol is 40,000 IU per week for 2 weeks.16,17 The mean
difference reported between baseline hemoglobin levels and those on the day of surgery is 1.1
g/dL.
Another proposed administration protocol is 600 IU/kg subcutaneously in a four-dose
regimen, 21 days, 14 days, 7 days, and 1 day preoperatively.18 With this protocol, the mean
difference between baseline and preoperative hemoglobin levels is 1.9 g/dL.
According to a 2016 meta-analysis, complications generally were not reported with the use of
EPO; however, no significant difference was observed between the groups with and without
EPO.19
The high cost of the medicine is a deterrent to its routine use.3,20
The use of EPO is recommended in patients at higher risk for allogenic transfusion, such as
those with low preoperative hemoglobin levels (<13 g/dL) or low body weight (<50 kg), and in
surgical procedures in which considerable blood loss is expected.3
Autologous Blood Donation

9/3/26, 7:31 AM
AAOS | Blood Management in Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001025
5/18

Autologous blood donation was initially introduced into clinical practice in the 1980s because
of the threat of viral pathogens with allogenic transfusions.21
This method involves the patient donating his or her own blood at least 3 weeks
preoperatively, which is then used postoperatively rather than an allogenic transfusion.
Advanced donation of blood allows patients’ hemoglobin levels to rise after blood donation
but preoperatively while also storing blood to be used rather than allogenic blood.
Autologous blood transfusion is not routinely used because studies have shown that
approximately 40% of the pre-donated units of blood were wasted.22 In addition, autologous
blood transfusion adds substantial costs to the episode of care.
Controversy exists surrounding preoperative autologous blood donation because it induces
anemia preoperatively, which has been shown to be one of the strongest risk factors for blood
transfusion. Anemia has been reported at a rate of 11% in patients undergoing THA and TKA
who donate blood preoperatively. The rate of anemia also increases with age.23
Patients who undergo THA after preoperative blood donation have higher transfusion rates
than those who do not donate blood.24
In addition, advanced planning, storage, and preparation of the donated units are
required.17,25
Concerns for clerical error, bacterial contamination, and infection also are associated with
autologous blood donation, and transfusion reactions to autologous blood have been
reported.9,26
The greatest advantage of preoperative autologous blood donation is observed in patients
with normal preoperative hemoglobin levels (>14 g/dL) who undergo surgical procedures in
which a considerable amount of blood loss is expected, such as revision procedures or
bilateral TKA.27
Intraoperative Management
Patient Positioning and Approach
Patient positioning may affect blood loss during various orthopaedic procedures because
incorrect positioning may lead to obstruction of venous return, resulting in vessel
engorgement and, eventually, increased blood loss during the procedure.27,28
For TKA, the patient is placed in the supine position, whereas for THA the patient may be
placed in the supine or lateral position depending on the approach. Placement of a patient

9/3/26, 7:31 AM
AAOS | Blood Management in Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001025
6/18

undergoing THA in the lateral position potentially reduces intraoperative blood loss.29
Conflicting data are available on the importance of surgical approach for THA, with some
studies showing smaller transfusion volumes and less blood loss in patients who undergo a
minimally invasive anterolateral approach compared with a posterolateral approach30 and
other studies showing no substantial differences between minimally invasive anterolateral and
minimally invasive posterior approaches.31 Regardless, the minimally invasive posterolateral
approach for THA is associated with the best reduction in blood loss.32-34
For the anterior approach, studies have reported statistically significant increases in blood loss
with the direct anterior approach compared with the mini-posterior approach.35 Compared
with the posterior approach in other studies, no difference was found regarding blood
loss.36,37
Use of a Tourniquet in TKA
For TKA, use of a tourniquet was reported by 95% of surgeons in 2010; however, interest in
tourniquetless TKA has increased38 (Resource 2). 
The advantages of a tourniquet include a bloodless field and less intraoperative blood loss;39
however, use of a tourniquet may increase postoperative hidden blood loss.40
Another potential advantage of not using a tourniquet in TKA is avoidance of reflex hyperemia
after deflation, which may increase blood loss. Regardless, a recent meta-analysis on
tourniquet use in TKA concluded that the use of a tourniquet may substantially decrease
intraoperative blood loss.41
Another option for tourniquet use is to inflate it only during cementation of the component.
Currently, no clear consensus exists on whether a tourniquet should be used for perioperative
management of blood loss during TKA.42
Reinfusion Systems
Reinfusion systems, in which the patient’s blood is collected during the procedure, also can be
used. These systems can filter and wash the shed blood for later reinfusion.
Advantages of these systems include reduced postoperative hematomas (similar to any drain
system), decreased wound complications, and alternative to allogenic blood.3
However, these systems are not without complications; coagulopathy and blood
contamination can occur, along with a substantially increased cost.3

The etiology of this coagulopathy is linked to the altered composition of the reinfused blood,
with reported elevations in fibrin split products and inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor
necrosis factor-alpha and interleukins.43,44
No clear consensus in the literature exists regarding the efficacy of these systems; however,
most studies report no substantial effect. Therefore, these systems are sparingly used in
routine total joint arthroplasty.43,44
Fibrin Sealant
Fibrin sealant promotes blood coagulation reactions via fibrinogen and thrombin to reduce
postoperative bleeding.45 In a 2014 meta-analysis, the use of fibrin sealants led to higher
postoperative hemoglobin levels, lower drainage volumes, lower transfusion rates, and
reduced hematomas.46
Conversely, controversy exists with regard to the use of fibrinogen in total joint arthroplasty
because a randomized clinical trial reported no difference in calculated blood loss between
patients who received intra-articular fibrinogen and those who did not.47 In addition, the cost
of using these fibrin sealants must be considered.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine may cause constriction of the vessels.
Intraoperative periarticular injections that contain epinephrine have been shown to reduce
blood loss.48
Anderson et al48 reported a decrease of 32% in drain collections after TKA in patients who
were administered epinephrine injections.
Tranexamic Acid
TXA has revolutionized modern blood management in THA and TKA by substantially reducing
blood loss and transfusion rates (Resource 3).
TXA is an antifibrinolytic agent and a synthetic derivative of the amino acid lysine, which may
inhibit the activation of plasminogen and the fibrin breakdown process.49
The administration of TXA can be intravenous, topical, or oral.
A common intravenous use is 1 g of TXA just before incision and 1 g intravenously 3 hours
later.7 Topical administration of TXA theoretically increases concentration at the surgical site

with reduced systemic exposure, reduces cost, and gives the surgeon control of
administration.50
Topical administration is not inferior to intravenous administration in terms of safety and
efficacy.6,51
TXA appears to be safe, even in high-risk patients, resulting in lower morbidity rates and no
increased risk of venous thromboembolic events.52
According to recent reports, TXA acts on the fibrinolytic pathway only and does not have a
prothrombotic effect, such as increasing formation of a thrombus.53
Bipolar Sealants
Contrary to standard monopolar electrocautery, bipolar sealants require the use of bipolar
radiofrequency.
A continuous flow of saline water is present with these devices, which does not allow the
temperature at the tip to increase.
As a result, shrinkage of the collagen in the vessels occurs, leading to decreased tissue
damage.3
Data are conflicting on the use of bipolar sealants, with some studies demonstrating a
reduction in blood loss54,55 and other studies not demonstrating reduction in blood loss.1,56
Surgical Time
Surgical time may directly influence blood loss and subsequent need for blood
transfusion.57,58
The correlation of surgical time and blood loss after THA or TKA is not well defined.
According to some studies, longer surgical procedures result in greater blood loss and a high
rate of transfusion.57-59
In addition, greater blood loss in revision procedures is to the result of longer surgical times
and more extensile approaches.60
Other studies have not shown a positive correlation between surgical time and blood loss.61,62
In a comparison of a minimally invasive TKA approach versus a standard approach, the
minimally invasive procedure had an increased surgical time without an increase in blood
loss.61

Drain Use
The exclusion of closed suction drains in total joint arthroplasty is becoming increasingly
accepted.
Apart from a higher risk of infection secondary to retrograde bacterial migration,63 closed
suction drains also have been associated with greater blood loss because the drain prevents
the tamponade effect.64
Randomized controlled trials present conflicting data on transfusion and the use of drains in
primary THA and TKA.
Studies have reported no statistically significant differences in transfusion rates in patients
with and without the use of a drain after TKA.65,66
Conversely, a randomized controlled trial proposed that patients with a drain after TKA had
increased postoperative blood loss compared with patients without a drain.67
In addition, a recent retrospective study reported that the use of a drain was associated with a
higher transfusion rate after THA and TKA.68
The findings of more current studies suggest that suction drains are not indicated in TKA, with
or without the use of TXA.69
Postoperative Management
Cryotherapy
After TKA, compression and cryotherapy usually are performed.
These techniques have proved to have a small effect on blood loss reduction.70,71
Despite the advantages of these systems, possible complications, such as coagulopathy and
infection/contamination, and cost should be considered.3
Continuous Suction Drains
In addition, lack of a suction drain is thought to minimize blood loss despite some surgeons
believing that placement of an intra-articular drain prevents hematoma and promotes
rehabilitation.7
Transfusion Triggers

The threshold at which a blood transfusion is administered is one of the most crucial factors
for postoperative blood management after total joint arthroplasty. In the past, patients used
to receive a transfusion if the hemoglobin level was less than 10 g/dL.
A practice that has been proposed is transfusion based on symptoms. According to
Robinson,72 this practice may lead to a 55% reduced transfusion rate.
In 2014, Levine et al3 recommend avoiding transfusion in any patient with a hemoglobin level
higher than 8 g/dL, whereas a hemoglobin level lower than 6 g/dL would trigger a transfusion.
Institutional blood transfusion guidelines should continually be reevaluated by a
multidisciplinary team based on the best available evidence.
With a comprehensive blood management strategy, transfusion rates after THA and TKA
should be approximately 1% to 2%.
Summary
A preoperative hemoglobin assessment and referral to hematology for a hemoglobin level
lower than 10 g/dL is recommended.
Ubiquitous use of TXA, tourniquet use, avoidance of drains, watertight multilayered wound
closure, occlusive dressing, compression, and cryotherapy should be considered as methods
to reduce blood loss.
Postoperative strict transfusion triggers and an emphasis on fluid resuscitation before blood
transfusion are recommended.
Mark as Complete
